summary: This program defines a RobotPet class that guards its battery level with a property, so any value assigned is clamped into the range 0 to 100. Three pets are created and their details printed.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Even inside the constructor, this assignment goes through the property setter rather than storing the value directly, so a bad starting battery is corrected right away.
The @property decorator turns the method below into a read-only attribute: readers write pet.battery, not pet.battery().
This getter hands back the internally stored value. The leading underscore in _battery signals that outside code should leave it alone and use the property instead.
This decorator registers the next method as the code that runs whenever something assigns to .battery, which is where the validation lives.
The setter receives the value being assigned and decides what actually gets stored.
Anything negative is treated as an empty battery rather than being rejected with an error.
Anything above full is capped, so the battery can never claim more charge than it holds.
A value already inside the valid range is stored unchanged.

lines.code: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
lines.text: A docstring documents what the method expects and returns; help(RobotPet.can_walk) will show this text.
Naming the calculation makes the rule visible, so the walking cost can be tuned in one place.
The comparison itself is either True or False, so it can be returned directly without an if statement.
Creating an instance runs __init__, which routes the battery value through the validating setter.
Reading pet1.battery quietly calls the getter, which is the point of encapsulation: the protection is invisible at the point of use.
